title: Logic and Fallacies

learn.summary: An argument is a set of premises offered in support of a conclusion — and the core skill is separating whether the logic holds from whether the premises are true. Informal logic gives names to the recurring ways arguments go wrong: attacking the person, torching a straw man, forcing false choices. Learn the patterns so you can diagnose reasoning, not so you can win by shouting Latin.

do: Take one opinion piece and rewrite its core argument as numbered premises and a conclusion; mark which premise you find weakest.

children.title: Arguments and Validity

learn.summary: A valid argument is one where the conclusion must be true if the premises are; a sound argument is valid and has true premises. This split matters: 'all cats are robots, robots can't purr, so cats can't purr' is perfectly valid and completely unsound. Most bad everyday arguments fail on premises, not logic — so check the inputs before fighting about the inference.

do: Write out 2 arguments you encountered this week in premise-conclusion form and label each: valid/invalid, and sound/unsound.

children.title: Common Fallacies

learn.summary: A handful of fallacies do most of the damage: ad hominem (attack the person), straw man (attack a distorted version of the claim), false dilemma (only two options presented), slippery slope (chain of doom with no probabilities), and appeal to nature. They persist because each is a corrupted version of a sometimes-legitimate move — character does matter for testimony; some slopes are slippery. The skill is telling the legitimate version from the fallacious one.

do: Collect 5 real fallacy examples from social media or comment sections this week and name the specific fallacy in each.

children.title: Fallacy-Hunting Pitfalls

learn.summary: The 'fallacy fallacy' is concluding a claim is false because someone argued for it badly — but true things get defended with terrible arguments all the time. Naming fallacies is also a favorite way to dodge substance ('that's a slippery slope, I win'). Use fallacy-spotting as a prompt to steelman and re-examine the claim, never as a conversation-ending trump card.

do: Find one claim you dismissed because of a bad argument for it, then spend 10 minutes constructing the best argument for that same claim.
